Female snakefish reach an ultimate total length of 32.6 centimeters [Li = 32.6 centimeters], a size attained after several years of steady somatic growth in the warm, productive waters of their continental shelf habitat. Analysis of length-frequency distributions from trawl surveys indicates that sexual maturation is initiated once individuals reach a total length at puberty of approximately 18 centimeters [Lp = approximately 18 centimeters], a threshold that aligns with the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation onset in males. Field collections of gravid females reveal that the wet weight at birth of the newly hatched larva is barely 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a mass derived from the egg diameter of roughly 0.8 millimeters and reflecting the extreme fecundity typical of this batch-spawning actinopterygian. The yolk-sac larva absorbs its endogenous reserves rapidly and transitions to first exogenous feeding within a few days, at which point the considerable mortality characteristic of the planktonic larval phase begins to shape the cohort's survivorship.

Reproductive output in this species is prodigious, yet tightly coupled to thermal conditions. At a stable 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], females release an average clutch of approximately 426,200 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 426,200 eggs per spawning event]. Throughout the peak of the breeding season, they can complete roughly 1.1 such events per day [F_R_i = roughly 1.1 such events per day], yielding an extraordinary daily reproductive rate. This maximum reproductive rate is among the highest recorded for any synodontid fish, an adaptation that offsets the tiny size and low survivorship of the pelagic eggs and early larvae. Each individual batch is broadcast into the water column during the evening hours, where fertilisation occurs externally and the fertilised ova drift as part of the ichthyoplankton community.

The wet weight of an adult female at her final size, or ultimate wet weight, reaches 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams], a value derived from allometric equations relating length to mass for this species, which supports the production of the enormous number of oocytes observed during each spawning event. The relationship between length and mass follows a steep power function, indicating that larger females invest disproportionately more in gonadal tissue than smaller conspecifics. This pattern is consistent with the life-history strategy of many tropical iteroparous teleosts, where fecundity scales positively with maternal size and condition. Adult females sampled during the pre-spawning period show considerable lipid accumulation in the viscera and muscle, suggesting that 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams] represents not only a morphological endpoint but also a reservoir of energy reserves necessary for repeated broadcast spawning bouts over the course of several weeks.

Life span in the snakefish, when considering individuals reared in captivity at a controlled thermal regime of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], has been documented at approximately 2,555 days [am = approximately 2,555 days]. This longevity is comparable to that observed for other small-bodied, short-lived members of the family Synodontidae inhabiting subtropical and tropical shelf ecosystems. The limited life span is likely an evolutionary response to high natural mortality from predation and the energetic demands of such a massive reproductive investment per unit time. Field mark-recapture studies corroborate the captive estimates, with the oldest wild individuals recovered seldom exceeding seven years. The synchrony between maximum longevity under captive conditions and the inferred life span in the field suggests that the species' physiological clock is tightly constrained by the metabolic costs of maintaining high fecundity at elevated temperatures. Senescence in older females is marked by a decline in oocyte quality and reduced fertilization success in the final spawning seasons before death.

The evolutionary ecology of the snakefish is shaped by the trade-offs inherent in its extreme reproductive schedule. By channeling resources into massive, frequent clutches rather than large offspring or extended parental care, the species conforms to a classic r-selected strategy. The extremely small mass of the yolk-sac larva at hatching is a direct consequence of this prioritization; dispersing millions of tiny propagules allows the population to exploit unpredictable recruitment windows in a variable planktonic environment. Comparative analysis with other synodontids indicates that the ultimate total length of 32.6 centimeters [Li = 32.6 centimeters] positions the snakefish as a medium-sized member of the genus, while the corresponding 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams] of adult body mass aligns closely with predictions from the length-weight relationship. Future studies examining metabolic scaling and reproductive effort across thermal gradients will further clarify how this species maintains such high population turnover rates in the face of warming ocean conditions.
